Anthropic shared early results from six drug development partners using Claude.
In one project, Claude produced about 35,000 antibody designs for food allergy research in roughly a month.
Other teams saw 10x more cancer-detecting receptors in lab tests and an 89% cut in paperwork review time.
Most of the work is preclinical and has not been tested in humans.

site_article.headline: Anthropic reports early drug development results from Claude with six partners

site_article.summary: Anthropic on October 27, 2026 published early results from six drug development partners using Claude, including about 35,000 antibody designs for food allergy research produced in roughly a month. The company also said it acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person startup working on rare forms of muscular dystrophy.
site_article.seo_title: Anthropic shares Claude drug development results with six partners
site_article.seo_description: Claude produced about 35,000 antibody designs in a month and cut drug paperwork review by 89 percent, Anthropic and its partners report. Work is preclinical.
site_article.answer_summary: Anthropic says Claude helped six drug developers design antibodies, improve a CAR T cell therapy and review manufacturing records much faster. The results are early and mostly preclinical, so no drug from this work has been tested in humans.
site_article.hero_alt: A scientist in a lab coat holds a rack of sample tubes in a cluttered lab while a robotic arm works behind her.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic on October 27, 2026 published early results from six outside organizations that are using its Claude models in drug development, along with its first in-house drug programs. The partners are BigHat Biosciences, Bristol Myers Squibb, Divergence Labs, Enveda, Generate Biomedicines and The Column Group, according to Becker's Hospital Review. Most of the work is preclinical, meaning none of the drug candidates have been tested in people.

The largest number in the update comes from Divergence Labs. Claude generated about 35,000 antibody designs in roughly a month, working mostly on its own after turning the research goals into a design plan, Interesting Engineering reported. Unite.AI said the work ran over 22 autonomous stretches and used about 2,750 Nvidia H100 GPU hours.

The project targets immunoglobulin E, or IgE, the antibody behind allergic reactions. Existing drugs mainly neutralize IgE in the bloodstream, while this approach aims to pull it off immune cells. In early lab results, three designs attached to IgE and 20 could dislodge it from immune cells. Three of those 20 appeared to clear more IgE than Xolair, a standard medication, at realistic concentrations, according to Anthropic. The two functions have not yet been combined into one molecule.

At Generate Biomedicines, six researchers used Claude Code to redesign part of the genetic instructions that control CAR T cells, a type of cancer therapy. One design was about 70 percent shorter than the standard version and produced roughly 10 times as many cancer-detecting receptors in lab tests. Interesting Engineering noted that the findings do not show effectiveness in patients.

BigHat Biosciences connected Claude to an automated lab system and tested about 1,010 antibody variants over roughly 10 weeks. Unite.AI reported that the final molecules bound their targets 6 to 9 times more tightly, and that both molecules became more stable at higher temperatures.

Enveda used Claude to review 1,061 pages of manufacturing records. Claude flagged all 11 issues that human reviewers had found plus seven more, and review time fell 89 percent, from more than 25 hours to under three. Becker's reported that Claude also drafted a regulatory document in four hours, a task that takes about three months by hand. Bristol Myers Squibb is using Claude to assess clinical trial plans for an early-stage drug, and the two companies plan to expand the work in 2027.

Anthropic also said it acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company founded by Cody Tranbarger that works on two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Tranbarger used Claude to coordinate work across 11 outside labs and took one candidate from idea to promising results in mice in under 18 months. He is continuing the research at Anthropic, and a drug could enter human trials as soon as late 2028 if the candidates hold up.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the update shows Anthropic moving from selling a general assistant to making specific claims about laboratory outcomes, and even owning a drug program. The results are reported by Anthropic and its partners, and they come from early lab and animal work. The gap between a promising molecule and an approved medicine is long, so speed gains in design and paperwork are the clearest takeaway for now.
The next milestone to watch is whether Divergence Labs can combine its two antibody functions into a single molecule, and whether Mithril names a clinical candidate in 2027 as planned.
